Sen. Chris Van Hollen Will Challenge Chuck Schumer for Senate Majority Leader
Nov 13, 2026
Link copied
Maryland Senator Chris Van Hollen said Thursday he will challenge New York’s Chuck Schumer for Senate majority leader when Democrats retake control of both chambers of Congress in January. This follows historic gains for Democrats in last week’s midterm elections. They’ll now control at least 255 seats in the House of Representatives and 55 in the Senate. This is Senator Van Hollen speaking on MS NOW.
Sen. Chris Van Hollen: “And it wasn’t only a rejection of Donald Trump and his corruption and his wars and his cruelty. It was also about a call for a larger change to take on a broken economic system that’s rigged in favor of the very wealthy against working people and that’s fueled by a corrupt political system. And the call was really to reject the status quo and to reject business as usual. And to do that, I think we need new leadership.”
Van Hollen is the first Democratic senator to launch a leadership challenge since 1994. His bid was quickly endorsed by Michigan Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed and Vermont independent Senator Bernie Sanders.

Youth Climate Activists Protest in Chuck Schumer’s Office to Demand New Senate Leadership
Nov 13, 2026
Image Credit: Artivista Karlin/Sunrise Movement
Link copied
More than 50 young activists with the Sunrise Movement were arrested Thursday after hundreds of protesters staged a sit-in inside Senator Chuck Schumer’s Washington, D.C., office. Activists are pushing for new Democratic leadership in the Senate after nearly a decade under Schumer. They also want Democrats to abolish the Senate filibuster. Children also participated in the action Thursday as many of the protesters held signs that read “The filibuster kills,” “Stop the climate crisis,” and “Schumer: Step up or step aside.”
Sunrise Movement activist 1: “Chuck Schumer and establishment Democrats are more scared of the voices of young people than of the climate crisis.”
Grace: “The American public is tired of the same old politics, and we’re ready for real change.”
Sunrise Movement activist 2: “Chuck Schumer would rather listen to billionaires than young people.”
Sunrise Movement activist 3: “Chuck Schumer doesn’t listen to us. He listens to corporate money, specifically coming from AIPAC. Over $400,000 have been invested into him.”
Jamie: “I chose to do this because when I was in high school, I saw the places I love burn to the ground because of the climate crisis. As I’ve grown older, I’ve seen American tax dollars go to burning and bombing Gaza.”
Grace: “I think everybody, including young people the most, can see the writing on the wall at this point, right? And we’re all saying the ship needs to be going in this direction.”

Nvidia’s Colette Kress to Serve as Interim CEO as Jensen Huang Resigns Amid Scandals
Nov 13, 2026
Link copied
Nvidia CEO and co-founder Jensen Huang has resigned. The chip maker says its longtime chief financial officer, Colette Kress, will serve as interim CEO while Nvidia’s board of directors searches for a permanent replacement. Huang stepped down as Reuters reported he’d had an intimate relationship with a second employee, whom Reuters did not name. That follows reports that Huang had an affair with a Chinese businesswoman who U.S. intelligence officials claim was spying for Beijing as part of a Chinese intelligence operation seeking to acquire advanced computer chips, which are banned by U.S. export controls. Huang reportedly helped the alleged spy acquire at least $7.5 billion worth of Nvidia chips for China via a Singapore-based cloud computing company called Megaspeed International. Meanwhile, Bloomberg reports Jensen Huang has agreed to testify before House lawmakers in a closed-door hearing later this month. Nvidia has lost nearly $2 trillion in market capitalization since its all-time high in early October. We’ll have more on this story after headlines.

Nov 13, 2026
Link copied
In more technology news, Microsoft is scrambling to fix a major outage that’s disrupted communication for millions of people across at least 74 countries since Thursday morning. The outage has cut off access to Microsoft’s Outlook, Teams and the AI assistant Copilot.

Iran Says It Blew Up U.S. Early-Warning Radar as Trump Declares, “We Don’t Need a Deal with Iran”
Nov 13, 2026
Link copied
Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps says it destroyed a U.S. early-warning radar system in Bahrain in retaliation for a U.S. strike on a telecommunications tower in southern Iran. Officials also claimed four attacks on oil tankers in ​the Strait of Hormuz on Thursday, following strikes on a pair of supertankers one day earlier.
Iran’s attacks came as President Trump on Thursday sidelined Vice President JD Vance as the top U.S. negotiator with Iran. Trump said in a social media post he’d directed Vance to instead focus on fighting what Trump called “corruption and crime” in Democratic-controlled cities and states. Trump wrote, “We don’t need a deal with Iran. Those days have long since passed. We’ve got their money, Hundreds of Billions of Dollars, and we’ve got their Strait!”

Houthis Claim Fresh Attacks on Saudi Oil Facilities Including East-West Pipeline
Nov 13, 2026
Link copied
Yemen’s Ansar Allah movement, known as the Houthis, has claimed fresh attacks on oil infrastructure and an air base in Saudi Arabia. A Houthi spokesperson said targets included the Yanbu oil facility on the Red Sea, an Aramco facility in Riyadh and a pumping station on the East-West Pipeline, which is Saudi Arabia’s main route for shipping oil past Iran’s blockade on the Strait of Hormuz. Meanwhile, the Arab League warned Thursday that a Houthi siege of the southwestern Yemeni city of Taiz is leading to a humanitarian disaster, with “acute shortages of fuel, oxygen, medicines and medical supplies.”

Russia and Ukraine Continue Deadly Strikes as U.S. Envoys Meet Putin and Zelensky
Nov 13, 2026
Link copied
Russia and Ukraine traded drone and missile attacks overnight, despite a diplomatic push by the Trump administration that’s purportedly seeking an end to the conflict. The violence came after President Trump’s envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner met with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow, followed by a meeting with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky in Dublin. Both Russia and Ukraine agreed to a prisoner swap that Zelensky called the largest since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Meanwhile, Zelensky has accused Elon Musk’s SpaceX of once again restricting service to Starshield, the military-grade version of the Starlink internet satellite constellation, which Ukraine uses for drone attacks.

Infant Dies of Hypothermia in Gaza as Calls Grow for Israel to Allow Imports of Winter Supplies
Nov 13, 2026
Image Credit: Deutsche Presse-Agentur GmbH
Link copied
In Gaza, a Palestinian infant has died from hypothermia after Israeli attacks left his family displaced and living in a tent in Khan Younis. Kinan Ahmed Raqiq was just 9 months old. His death came as Israel continued to impose severe restrictions on imports of fuel and winter supplies into Gaza. U.N. humanitarian chief Tom Fletcher says 150,000 tents remain stuck in warehouses at Gaza’s borders, even as some 350,000 displaced Palestinians face heavy rain, flooding and plummeting temperatures. On Thursday, a group of 49 nations issued a joint call for Israel to ease restrictions on shelter, fuel, water, sanitation and medical supplies to Gaza. The United States did not sign the statement. This is Britain’s ambassador to the U.N., Sarah MacIntosh, speaking from U.N. headquarters.
Sarah MacIntosh: “As winter sets in, far too many people in Gaza are still without adequate shelter and risk exposure to hypothermia, respiratory infections, waterborne diseases and other preventable illnesses. Constraints on the entry of critical shelter items and other life-saving supplies continue to prevent humanitarian organizations from responding at the scale required.”
In more news from Gaza, a Palestinian was killed by Israeli gunfire east of Gaza City earlier today. That followed an Israeli strike on a car near the gate of Al-Shifa Hospital which killed one person and left several others critically wounded. That attack came as Palestinians in Khan Younis held funerals for a ​surgeon, a teenage boy and four other Palestinians killed when an Israeli airstrike targeted southern Gaza’s Nasser Hospital complex. We’ll have more on that attack, and the latest from Gaza, later in the broadcast.

ICE Detention of USF Professor Draws Protests and Demands for Her Release
Nov 13, 2026
Image Credit: University of San Francisco
Link copied
In California, community members are demanding the release of beloved nurse and University of San Francisco professor Ann Lawani, who was detained by ICE nearly two months ago. Lawani is originally from Nigeria and has lived in the U.S. since 2007. She was reportedly at home in Lodi, still wearing her pajamas, when ICE agents showed up at her door in early September, taking her to a local holding facility. Then she disappeared from ICE’s database for three days, with her older brother telling The New York Times, “It was the worst time of my life, knowing she had been siphoned into an abyss and there was nothing I could do about it.” Lawani is now being detained thousands of miles away at an ICE jail in Basile, Louisiana.

Hundreds of protesters, including teachers and elected officials, rallied outside San Diego’s federal building Thursday, calling for an 8-year-old Haitian boy to be reunited with his relatives. He was taken into federal immigration custody after a check-in last week. The boy is a third grader at a local elementary school. His family and advocates say they do not know his whereabouts.

23 Immigrants Died of Medical Neglect in ICE Custody in First Year of Trump’s Second Term
Nov 13, 2026
Image Credit: GEO Group
Link copied
Nearly two dozen immigrants died in the custody of ICE during the first year of President Trump’s second term due to medical neglect. That’s according to findings by the San Francisco Chronicle, which obtained internal ICE investigations into the 29 deaths that occurred in 2025. ICE’s own documents admit immigration jails failed to provide emergency medical care. In some cases, ICE jail staff even mocked or ignored people who requested help and who later died.
At least 62 immigrants have died in ICE custody since Trump’s return to office. In response to the abuse, immigrants jailed across the nation have staged hunger strikes and other peaceful actions. This week, the publication L.A. Taco reported at least 24 people detained at the Adelanto ICE jail in California’s Mojave Desert started another hunger strike — the second so far this year. Meanwhile, another hunger strike at the Northwest ICE jail in Tacoma, Washington, is also ongoing. Hunger strikers at both facilities have reportedly faced threats, including being transferred to other ICE jails across the country. Both Adelanto and Northwest are operated by the for-profit prison company GEO Group.

NYC Mayor Mamdani Orders Inspections at 100 Sites After Deadly Building Collapse in Brooklyn
Nov 13, 2026
Link copied
Here in New York, tenant advocates are demanding justice after what they described as the preventable collapse of an apartment building in Brooklyn that killed at least eight people, including two children, and injured at least 23 others Wednesday. Among the victims were two construction workers from Ecuador and Guatemala; a food delivery worker and Amazon worker, who were relatives from Guinea in West Africa; and two young cousins from Colombia.
The publication amNewYork reports the collapse may have been caused by corner-cutting by subcontractors and developers working on an adjacent construction site where crews were digging a pit for a new massive, multi-story development. In the wake of the collapse, New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani said five contractors and developers connected to the disaster are associated with about 100 other sites across New York, and that the Department of Buildings would immediately begin inspecting those sites.
The executive director of NYS Tenant Bloc, Sumathy Kumar, said in a statement that the tragedy “stresses the urgency of taking buildings out of the hands of bad landlords who are looking to make quick profits at the expense of people’s safety” and “highlights the need for dignified, high quality housing built with union labor, which is why we are fighting for social housing across the city and state.”

El senador Chris Van Hollen anuncia que desafiará a Chuck Schumer por el liderazgo de la mayoría demócrata en el Senado de EE.UU.
13 Nov. 2026
Link copied
El senador del estado de Maryland Chris Van Hollen anunció el jueves que se enfrentará al senador de Nueva York Chuck Schumer por el liderazgo de la mayoría del Senado de Estados Unidos, una vez que los demócratas recuperen el control de ambas cámaras del Congreso en enero del próximo año. Esto se produce tras los logros históricos conseguidos por los demócratas en las elecciones de mitad de mandato de la semana pasada. Los demócratas han obtenido al menos 255 escaños en la Cámara de Representantes y 55 en el Senado. Estas fueron las palabras expresadas por el senador Van Hollen, en declaraciones al canal de televisión MS NOW.
Senador Chris Van Hollen: “No fue solo un rechazo a Donald Trump, su corrupción, sus guerras y su crueldad. También fue un llamado a impulsar un cambio más grande para hacer frente a un sistema económico quebrado, que está amañado a favor de los muy ricos en detrimento de los trabajadores y se sustenta en un sistema político corrupto. Fue realmente un llamado para rechazar el 'statu quo' y las prácticas de siempre. Para responder a ese llamado, creo que necesitamos un nuevo liderazgo”.
Van Hollen es el primer senador demócrata desde 1994 que presenta una candidatura para disputar el liderazgo del partido en la Cámara Alta. El senador electo del estado de Michigan Abdul El-Sayed y el senador independiente del estado de Vermont Bernie Sanders expresaron rápidamente su apoyo a la candidatura de Hollen.
Temas:
Partido Demócrata
Jóvenes activistas ambientales protestan en la oficina de Chuck Schumer para exigir un nuevo liderazgo en el Senado de EE.UU.
13 Nov. 2026
Image Credit: Artivista Karlin/Sunrise Movement
Link copied
Más de 50 jóvenes activistas de la organización ambientalista Sunrise Movement fueron arrestados el jueves después de que cientos de manifestantes realizaran una sentada de protesta dentro de la oficina del senador estadounidense Chuck Schumer en Washington D.C. Los activistas reclaman un nuevo liderazgo en el bloque demócrata del Senado estadounidense tras casi una década bajo la conducción de Schumer, y piden que los demócratas eliminen la regla del obstruccionismo legislativo en esa cámara. Varios menores de edad también participaron en la movilización del jueves, en las que muchos manifestantes portaban carteles con consignas como: “El obstruccionismo mata”, “Detengan la crisis climática” y “Schumer: dé un paso al frente o hágase a un lado”.
Activista 1 de Sunrise Movement: “Chuck Schumer y los dirigentes demócratas tienen más miedo a las voces de los jóvenes que a la crisis climática”.
Grace: “La población estadounidense está cansada de la misma política de siempre y está lista para un cambio real”.
Activista 2 de Sunrise Movement: “Chuck Schumer prefiere escuchar a los multimillonarios antes que a los jóvenes”.
Activista 3 de Sunrise Movement: “Chuck Schumer no nos escucha. Él escucha al dinero corporativo, en particular al que proviene del AIPAC [Comité Israelí-Estadounidense de Asuntos Públicos]. Han invertido más de 400.000 dólares en él”.
bq. Jamie: “Decidí hacer esto porque, cuando estaba en la escuela secundaria, vi cómo lugares que tanto quiero quedaban reducidos a cenizas a causa de la crisis climática. Con el paso de los años, he visto también cómo el dinero de los contribuyentes estadounidenses se destinaba a incendiar y bombardear Gaza”.
Grace: “Creo que todos, especialmente los jóvenes, pueden ver lo que se avecina a estas alturas, ¿verdad? Y todos estamos diciendo que el barco tiene que cambiar de rumbo”.

Colette Kress asume como directora ejecutiva interina de Nvidia tras la renuncia de Jensen Huang en medio de los escándalos
13 Nov. 2026
Link copied
El director ejecutivo y cofundador de la empresa tecnológica Nvidia, Jensen Huang, ha dimitido de su cargo. La empresa fabricante de chips informó que Colette Kress, directora financiera de la empresa desde hace mucho tiempo, ocupará de manera interina el puesto de directora ejecutiva hasta que la junta directiva de Nvidia encuentre un sucesor definitivo. Huang renunció después de que la agencia de noticias Reuters informara que había mantenido una relación íntima con una segunda empleada de la empresa, cuya identidad la agencia no reveló. Esto se produce después de que se informara que Huang mantuvo una relación extramatrimonial con una empresaria china que, según funcionarios de inteligencia estadounidenses, espiaba para Pekín como parte de una operación china para adquirir chips informáticos avanzados, cuya exportación está prohibida por las autoridades estadounidenses. Según trascendió, Huang ayudó a la presunta espía a conseguir para China chips de Nvidia por un valor de al menos 7.500 millones de dólares, a través de una empresa de computación en la nube con sede en Singapur llamada Megaspeed International. Mientras tanto, el medio de comunicación Bloomberg informa que Jensen Huang aceptó testificar ante legisladores de la Cámara de Representantes de Estados Unidos en una audiencia a puerta cerrada que se llevará a cabo en el correr de este mes. La empresa Nvidia ha perdido casi dos billones de dólares de capitalización bursátil desde que alcanzó su máximo histórico a principios de octubre. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned Thursday after reports of multiple extramarital affairs, including with an employee and a Chinese businesswoman whom U.S. intelligence officials accuse of spying for Beijing. The company says Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress will serve as interim CEO as the board searches for a permanent replacement.
Nvidia’s computer chips are at the heart of the artificial intelligence boom, driving the company’s value above $4 trillion and making Huang one of the most influential business leaders in the world. His spectacular fall from the company he co-founded in 1993 comes as the U.S. stock market has become highly dependent on a handful of AI-related companies and amid intense competition between the United States and China over control of the technology, with access to Nvidia’s chips becoming a major point of contention between the two countries.
Tech critic Paris Marx notes that the AI industry’s “circular financing,” in which companies are both clients and investors for one another, has created systemic risk.
We also speak with Ramesh Srinivasan, director of the AI Futures Lab at UCLA, who says the “soap opera” of the Huang scandal has exposed “how precarious the governance of this AI truly is,” with only a handful of people and firms controlling “incredibly powerful technology that feeds off of all of us and the planet.”

Transcript
This is a rush transcript. Copy may not be in its final form.
AMY GOODMAN: We begin today’s show looking at the fallout from Jensen Huang’s resignation as the CEO of Nvidia, one of the world’s most powerful companies. Nvidia’s advanced AI computer chips have powered much of the artificial intelligence boom. Huang cultivated close ties to President Trump and is credited with helping to shape U.S. policies around artificial intelligence and rules around the export of advanced AI chips.
Huang’s resignation came days after reports emerged he had an affair with a Chinese businesswoman named Alice Huang — no relation — whom U.S. intelligence officials reportedly suspected of spying for Beijing and helping China obtain advanced Nvidia chips, which are banned by U.S. export controls. The Information news outlet reports Alice Huang helped route at least $7.5 billion worth of Nvidia chips to China via a Singapore-based cloud computing company called Megaspeed International. Jensen Huang confirmed he had an affair with the woman. Later, published reports revealed he also had affairs with two employees at Nvidia, including with a senior executive who reported to him.
Nvidia has announced its longtime chief financial officer, Colette Kress, would serve as interim CEO as the board searches for a permanent replacement.
On Thursday, U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche took questions about Nvidia.
REPORTER: When did the Justice Department learn, with regard to Nvidia, that Alice Huang might be a suspected Chinese asset? And there’s been concerns raised that the Commerce Department was giving favoritism to Nvidia and Megaspeed, which is Alice Huang’s company. Do you share the concerns that maybe the Commerce Department was impeding the ability to uncover the smuggling network that Alice Huang was involved in?
ATTORNEY GENERAL TODD BLANCHE: Well, your first question assumes something that I have never said and that I don’t know to be true. So, you assume that DOJ learns that she is, in fact, a spy. I’m not — nobody said that. I certainly haven’t said that. And I don’t — all I said a minute ago, and all that I think I will say, is that, of course, DOJ is investigating or looking at it. So, there’s no — there’s no conclusions reached by the Department of Justice or by me or by Director Patel around who she is or is not.
I don’t have concerns with the Commerce Department. I don’t. We have a good relationship with the Commerce Department.

Israel’s latest bombing of Nasser Hospital in Gaza on Thursday killed six Palestinians, including surgeon Dr. Rizk Abu Shaira. He was featured in the recent documentary American Doctor, which follows international medical volunteers in Gaza’s battered hospitals as they work alongside Palestinian colleagues.
Israel claimed, without providing evidence, that it targeted a senior Hamas militant in the hospital strike. Israel has repeatedly bombed medical facilities in Gaza since the start of the genocide in October 2023, even though such attacks are prohibited under international law.
“It’s just barbarism. I don’t know why we’re supporting this,” says Dr. Feroze Sidhwa, one of the titular American doctors in the documentary, who demands accountability for Israel’s actions and a change in U.S. policy toward the country. “That’s an American-made bomb dropped by an American-made airplane burning American-supplied jet fuel.”
Sidhwa also comments on the catastrophic flooding in Gaza that has swamped the temporary shelters of tens of thousands of displaced Palestinians as Israel continues to block the entry of shelter materials into the territory. As a result, “babies are going to die of hypothermia in Gaza for the fourth year in a row,” Sidhwa says.

AMY GOODMAN: This is Democracy Now!, democracynow.org. I’m Amy Goodman.
In Gaza, funerals have been held for a surgeon, a teenage boy and four other Palestinians killed when an Israeli airstrike targeted the Nasser Hospital complex in southern Gaza. The surgeon was killed in the strike, Dr. Rizk Abu Shaira, featured in the recent documentary American Doctor. Footage filmed inside the hospital revealed severe destruction, rooms littered with debris and overturned furniture, cables hanging from broken ceilings, injured patients moved on stretchers through hallways covered in rubble.
NBC reports debris photographed at the scene shows fragments of a GBU-39 small diameter bomb produced by the U.S. aerospace and weapons manufacturer Boeing.
This is Dr. Ayman Abu Obeid, who was working an overnight shift and resting in a staff room when the explosion hit, leaving his right foot badly injured.
DR. AYMAN ABU OBEID: [translated] As usual, we were on shift at the hospital. We have rooms where we stay. We were surprised by a strike directly on the room we sleep in. Total destruction. No light left, no help left, no… I don’t know what happened. All of a sudden, the world turned upside down. It went dark all at once. Honestly, it was very terrifying.

As Democrats prepare to take control of Congress in January, party leaders say they intend to hold Trump officials accountable with stepped-up hearings and investigations. The administration, however, has responded with threats to launch its own investigations into lawmakers for carrying out their oversight responsibilities.
“The oversight function of Congress is well established by the founders. It’s a normal part of government. The separation of powers requires oversight,” says Brad Adams, co-founder of The Rule of Law Project, which seeks to provide outside accountability due to what he describes as the administration’s refusal to investigate “obvious cases of corruption.”

AMY GOODMAN: This is Democracy Now!, democracynow.org. I’m Amy Goodman.
Democrats have made clear their intentions to increase oversight and investigations into President Trump and administration officials in the next Congress. After Democrats secured the incoming majority in the midterm elections, the top-ranking Democrat on the House Oversight and Government Reform Committee, Congressmember Robert Garcia, released a statement, saying only, “Lawyer up.”
On Monday, the top White House lawyer, Will Scharf, sent Garcia a letter warning Democrats’ language and plans for investigations and subpoenas, quote, “may cross the line into blatant criminality.” He also wrote, quote, “The Administration will not be extorted and will not be cowed by unlawful process motivated by animus, pettiness, hatred, or any other unlawful motive,” the White House lawyer said.
For more on this brewing legal battle, we’re joined by Brad Adams, co-founder of The Rule of Law Project, a new organization formed by former federal civil rights and corruption prosecutors and investigators.
Brad, thanks so much for being with us. Can you first respond to the White House saying that if congressmembers engage in oversight, they might cross the line into criminality?
BRAD ADAMS: Yeah, it’s a bit rich, isn’t it? The oversight function of Congress is well established by the founders. It’s a normal part of government. The separation of powers requires oversight.
And what is, you know, ironic, of course, is that the Republicans have tried to weaponize the oversight process for many years. Think back to Benghazi and, you know, other high-profile efforts to harass the Biden administration or the Obama administration or some members of the Cabinet, such as Hillary Clinton. And I’ll point out, I’m not sure that Will Scharf wants — realizes this, but the newly elected leader of the minority in the House, Jim Jordan, was the chair of the House Judiciary Committee, and in that role, he issued 91 subpoenas to Democratic administrations. And many of those were clearly just meant to be political grandstanding, to harass, to get in the newspaper.
The Supreme Court in 2020 issued a ruling on this, and they said there are limits on oversight. And they basically said one key point — made one key point, which is that there has to be a clear legislative purpose. And what Representative Garcia is suggesting has a clear legislative purpose: to ensure that corruption doesn’t go unchecked, to look into ICE violence, killings, beatings on the streets, custodial mistreatment in ICE detention facilities, etc.
So, I mean, this statement, basically, you know, makes a lawyer who went to Harvard — that’s Will Scharf, went to Harvard — appear that he never took constitutional law classes.
AMY GOODMAN: And can you also respond to Todd Blanche, the attorney general, responding to Garcia, who is talking about everyone, from Stephen Miller on, to lawyer up? And he said, “I’m Stephen Miller’s lawyer. He doesn’t need to hire one.” What does that mean? I thought the attorney general was the people’s attorney. He was even questioned about this at his confirmation hearing, and he said he wasn’t, for example, Trump’s lawyer — which he used to be, of course.
BRAD ADAMS: Yeah, well, you can say one thing during confirmation hearings and then act in another way later. Oscar-nominated filmmaker James Longley talks about his new documentary Mohabat, named after a 12-year-old Afghan boy whose father was killed in a U.S. drone strike in 2019. Longley has filmed for years in Afghanistan both during the U.S. war and since the Taliban regained power. His previous films include Iraq in Fragments and Sari’s Mother, both of which received Academy Award nominations. His first feature-length documentary was Gaza Strip, released in 2002.

Transcript

AMY GOODMAN: This is Democracy Now!, democracynow.org, The War and Peace Report. I’m Amy Goodman, with Anjali Kamat.
ANJALI KAMAT: We turn now to the Oscar-nominated filmmaker James Longley, who’s filmed for years in Afghanistan, both during the U.S. war and since the Taliban regained power. James Longley’s new film is Mohabat. It is named after a 12-year-old Afghan boy whose father was killed in a U.S. drone strike in 2019. This is a clip from the film featuring Mohabat.
MOHABAT: [translated] When the Americans came here, wherever they went, a drone was always with them. When the drone was flying, everyone was afraid. The sound of them was awful. Every person thought they would be the one targeted. I thought they would bomb me.
AMY GOODMAN: In this next clip from Mohabat, several young Afghan boys talk about how their fathers were killed during the U.S. occupation.
AFGHAN BOY 1: [translated] A night raid came. They killed my father and dragged him behind their Humvee.
AFGHAN BOY 2: [translated] My father was Taliban. I was young when he was killed.
AFGHAN BOY 3: [translated] The helicopter shot my father, and he fell out of a tree.
AFGHAN BOY 4: [translated] My father was killed by a drone strike on the second day of Eid.
AFGHAN BOY 5: [translated] My father and his friend went to fight in the war. The Americans ambushed and killed them.
AFGHAN BOY 6: [translated] It was night when they brought him home.
AFGHAN BOY 7: [translated] My father was talking on his mobile, crossing the Wardak mountains.
AFGHAN BOY 8: [translated] A drone fired at him.
AFGHAN BOY 9: [translated] They buried him with an excavator on a mountainside in Nerkh district.
AMY GOODMAN: That’s a clip from James Longley’s new documentary Mohabat. The film is having its North American premiere at the DOC NYC Film Festival here in New York this weekend. James Longley’s previous films include Iraq in Fragments and Sari’s Mother, both of which received Academy Award nominations. His first feature-length documentary was Gaza Strip, released in 2002.
And I remember interviewing you then, James. What an honor it is to have you back with this deeply moving documentary. It features one boy, but it’s about three sons of an Afghan man who was killed in a U.S. drone strike. Tell us the story and how you found them. You’ve lived in Afghanistan for years.
JAMES LONGLEY: Well, I had been in Afghanistan for three-and-a-half years during the war. And when the Taliban took over, for a few months, like a lot of other people, we were working to get my crew members from the previous film out of the country, because at that time people were quite afraid of the Taliban, and no one knew what was going to happen.
AMY GOODMAN: And yet, you say that you knew for years, interviewing people, that people were saying, when the U.S. pulled out, the Taliban would take over.
JAMES LONGLEY: Yes. In my previous film, Angels Are Made of Light, many people say that they’re worried that the Taliban is going to come, that the Americans will leave and the Taliban will come back. And I also thought that, because it seemed quite obvious that the United States wasn’t going to be in Afghanistan forever, and that when they left, the only real possibility was that the Taliban would take over. It would either be a civil war followed by the Taliban, or just an immediate takeover. And years in advance, Afghan people who I trusted were telling me that the situation would change very quickly, and that when the United States left, they probably wouldn’t even make it all the way out of the country before the government fell.
So, in the beginning of 2022, I was able to get a visa and go back to Afghanistan and, once in Afghanistan, extend all of my documents. And we wound up staying there for two years, 15 months on the ground filming this documentary. And we traveled all over Afghanistan, location scouting and sort of casting the film, looking for the right people to follow. So, it gave me an opportunity to see Afghanistan in a way that I hadn’t before.

Democrat Scott Colom has made history as Mississippi’s first Democratic senator since 1982 — and its first African American senator since the post-Civil War Reconstruction era. Colom narrowly defeated Republican incumbent Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith in a state that President Trump won by nearly 23 points in 2024. Colom’s victory brings the incoming Senate Democratic caucus to 55. Colom gave his victory speech on Wednesday at the historically Black Tougaloo College, just miles from where civil rights activist Medgar Evers was murdered in 1963 by a member of the Ku Klux Klan.
“There were times that I couldn’t get donors to answer the phone; they did not believe a moment like this was possible. But I kept the faith,” said Colom. “There are so many people that had faith in Mississippi at times where it seemed impossible, people like Medgar Evers.”

This is a rush transcript. Copy may not be in its final form.
NERMEEN SHAIKH: We begin today’s show in Mississippi, where Democrat Scott Colom has defeated Republican Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith in a stunning upset. Colom is set to become the state’s first Democratic senator in 44 years and Mississippi’s first Black senator since post-Civil War Reconstruction. Colom’s election after three years — comes three years after Cindy Hyde-Smith blocked Colom’s nomination to a federal judgeship. In 2024, President Trump won Mississippi by nearly 23 points.
AMY GOODMAN: On Wednesday, Scott Colom gave his victory speech at the historically Black Tougaloo College. He spoke just miles from where civil rights activist Medgar Evers was murdered in 1963 by a member of the Ku Klux Klan.
SEN.-ELECT SCOTT COLOM: God bless you. For me, this journey started with a prayer, y’all. And in the Mississippi, our prayers have often changed the course of history.
For people that don’t know, the first African American to be a United States senator was from the great state of Mississippi. His name was Hiram Revels. And the way he got to be a United States senator was he was a minister in Natchez, Mississippi. He was elected to be in the state House, and when they were trying to figure out who was going to do the opening prayer, someone suggested Hiram Revels. He gave a prayer that was so powerful that people at that convention decided that he had a voice to be United States senator. That’s an example of the power of prayer.
And throughout our history, there are so many people that lifted this state up through the power of prayer in very dark times. But we all know that prayer is only a part of our Mississippi faith tradition. You need faith.
And I’ll tell you, throughout this campaign, there were many times where I had to have faith. There were times that I couldn’t get donors to answer the phone; they did not believe a moment like this was possible. But I kept the faith. There were times when I did my first town hall in Jackson, Mississippi. Frank Figgers helped me organize it. Less than 10 people showed up. But I kept the faith. I kept the faith. There were times when I was tired, and I felt like I couldn’t keep going. But I kept the faith.
And that is another tradition of our state. There’s so many people that had faith in Mississippi at times where it seemed impossible, people like Medgar Evers. I can’t help but think about Medgar Evers on Veterans Day, a moment like this, where he served his country and came home to Mississippi, when they wouldn’t let him vote. But he had faith that Mississippi could make progress. He had faith that one day everybody would have the right to vote. He had faith that a day like this was possible. God bless you, Medgar. God bless you, Medgar. God bless you.
When you talk about faith, you can’t forget Fannie Lou Hamer, who had faith that her being sick and tired could move a nation to understand that places like Mississippi have to matter, who had faith that even after she became a national celebrity and she could have gone anywhere in the world, she came right back to Mississippi. Petition Urging Jeffries to Remove Himself from Race to Become House Speaker Surpasses a Million Signatures
HeadlineNov 09, 2026
Link copied
Calls from progressives demanding new leadership in Congress continue to grow. An online petition urging Democratic Congressmember Hakeem Jeffries to remove himself from the running to become the next House speaker has surpassed 1 million signatures. Jeffries has faced mounting opposition over his pro-Israel interests and continued acceptance of corporate PAC money, including from the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, AIPAC. Several incoming progressive Congressmembers have not yet decided on whether to support Jeffries for House Speaker.
Chuck Schumer is facing similar calls to step down as Senate Democratic leader. Senators-elect Peggy Flanagan, Troy Jackson, Abdul El-Sayed, Juliana Stratton and Adam Hamilton have all said they won’t support Schumer.
